title: How the Movies Learned to Love Christians
author: Germán S. Díaz del Castillo
content:
![How the Movies Learned to Love
Christians](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-13-at-6.30.05
---AM.png)

When the film _God 's Not Dead_ was released in 2014, it was panned by
critics. The film follows a Christian college student who is told to renounce
his faith or fail a class. In addition to mocking the film's performances,
script, and production value, critics aimed fire at its plot, which they
dismissed as an unrealistic portrayal of the predicament of Christians in the
West. The following year, the Norwegian authorities forcibly removed the five
children of the Bodnariu family from their parents in what many have called a
case of anti-Christian persecution. The family's story serves as a basis for
Cristian Mungiu's new drama, _Fjord._ And while _God 's Not Dead _received no
mainstream awards, _Fjord_ won the Palme d'Or at Cannes, arguably the most
prestigious award in cinema.

The plot follows Romanian Mihai Gheorghiu, his wife Lisbet, and their
children, who relocate to Norway, Lisbet's birthplace, to be closer to her
family. The devoutly evangelical family (the film's stand-in for the Bodnariu
family) initially receives a warm welcome, but is soon thrust into a legal and
bureaucratic nightmare when Norway's version of Child Protective Services,
suspecting the parents of physical abuse, removes the five Gheorghiu children,
including their still-breastfeeding baby.
